---
title: "Faster PyMC: samplers × E₁"
---

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from _lib import *
B = read("bench_logp.csv", main=False)
F = read("fits.csv", main=False)
P = read("params.csv", main=False)

SAMPLERS = [("pymc", "pm.sample"), ("pymc-nutpie", "nutpie"), ("pymc-numpyro", "NumPyro")]
E1S = [("iid", "exact"), ("iid-fast", "fast"), ("iid-approx", "Swamee–Ohija")]
SCOLOR = {"pymc": COLOR["stan"], "pymc-nutpie": COLOR["pymc"], "pymc-numpyro": COLOR["turing"]}
ESYM = {"iid": "circle", "iid-fast": "diamond", "iid-approx": "square"}
V = F[F["backend"].isin([s for s, _ in SAMPLERS]) & F["errmodel"].isin([e for e, _ in E1S])].copy()
V["sampler"] = V["backend"].map(dict(SAMPLERS))
V["E1"] = V["errmodel"].map(dict(E1S))
V["iters"] = V["n_chains"] * 2000  # 1000 warmup + 1000 draws per chain
V["grads_per_iter"] = V["n_grad_evals"] / V["iters"]
```

The [backend comparison](backends.qmd) used PyMC's default NUTS sampler. Here
the **same PyMC model** is run with three different NUTS samplers and three
$E_1$ implementations, on all 11 spectra (iid error model). Like everything
else on this site, each fit uses one core with chains run one after another.

| Sampler | Log-density + gradient | Sampler loop |
|---|---|---|
| **pm.sample** | PyTensor → Numba (default backend) | PyMC's NUTS, in Python |
| **nutpie** | the same Numba-compiled function | Rust (`nuts-rs`) |
| **NumPyro** | PyTensor → JAX, gradient by JAX | the whole NUTS loop compiled by JAX/XLA (CPU) |

| $E_1$ | Implementation | Gradient |
|---|---|---|
| **exact** | Cephes `exp1` (SciPy for Numba; `jax.scipy.special.exp1` for JAX) | analytic, $-e^{-x}/x$ |
| **fast** | NAG S13AAF Chebyshev expansions from the original PROSPECT Fortran: two fixed-length polynomials, relative error ≤ 2×10⁻¹² | analytic, $-e^{-x}/x$ |
| **Swamee–Ohija** | closed form, relative error ~10⁻³ | automatic differentiation |

The fast $E_1$ changes PROSPECT-D R and T by ≤ 6×10⁻¹⁵ (see
[Forward model](verification.qmd)), so it is a drop-in replacement for the
exact one.

## Cost of one log-density + gradient

```{python}
#| label: fig-bench
#| fig-cap: "Single-threaded microbenchmarks on lopex_01 (2101 bands): E₁ alone (left) and the full log-density + gradient (right), for PyTensor's Numba backend (used by pm.sample and nutpie) and its JAX backend (used by NumPyro). Log scale; hover for values."
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=["E₁ only (µs)", "log-density + gradient (µs)"],
                    horizontal_spacing=0.1)
for ci, what in enumerate(("E1 only", "log-density + gradient")):
    for fw, col in (("numba", COLOR["stan"]), ("JAX", COLOR["pymc"])):
        d = B[(B["what"] == what) & (B["framework"] == fw)].set_index("e1").reindex(["exact", "fast", "approx"])
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=["exact", "fast", "Swamee–Ohija"], y=d["us"], name=fw, legendgroup=fw,
                             showlegend=(ci == 0), marker=dict(color=col, line=dict(color=SURFACE, width=2)),
                             text=[f"{v:,.0f}" for v in d["us"]], textposition="outside",
                             hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:,.0f} µs<extra>" + fw + "</extra>"), 1, ci + 1)
fig.update_yaxes(type="log", title_text="µs (log scale)", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(type="log", row=1, col=2)
fig.update_layout(barmode="group", height=420, legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.15, x=0), bargap=0.25)
show(fig)
b = B.set_index(["what", "framework", "e1"])["us"]
```

```{python}
t = B.pivot_table(index=["what", "e1"], columns="framework", values="us").reset_index()
show_table(fmt_table(t.rename(columns={"what": "Quantity", "e1": "E₁", "numba": "Numba (µs)", "JAX": "JAX (µs)"}), 3))
```

* **E₁ is about a quarter of the Numba gradient cost.** The fast E₁ cuts E₁
  from `{python} f"{b['E1 only','numba','exact']:.0f}"` to
  `{python} f"{b['E1 only','numba','fast']:.0f}"` µs. The full
  log-density + gradient drops from
  `{python} f"{b['log-density + gradient','numba','exact']:.0f}"` to
  `{python} f"{b['log-density + gradient','numba','fast']:.0f}"` µs.
* **JAX's built-in `exp1` is very slow on CPU**: `{python} f"{b['E1 only','JAX','exact']:,.0f}"` µs
  for 2101 values, about `{python} f"{b['E1 only','JAX','exact']/b['E1 only','numba','exact']:.0f}"`×
  Cephes. It evaluates a fixed number of series and continued-fraction
  iterations for every element. Swapping in the fast E₁ makes the JAX gradient
  `{python} f"{b['log-density + gradient','JAX','exact']/b['log-density + gradient','JAX','fast']:.0f}"`× faster.
* **Swamee–Ohija is the slowest option in both frameworks.** Its value is cheap
  to compute, but automatic differentiation through its `log`/`pow`/`exp`
  chain costs more than the exact function with an analytic gradient. Stan
  showed the same effect ([Backends](backends.qmd)).
* With the fast E₁, the remaining cost is the rest of PROSPECT (`exp`, `pow`,
  `sqrt` and about ten divisions per band). Fusing everything into one
  hand-written Numba loop does **not** help: 2101 bands fit in cache, so the
  cost is arithmetic, not memory traffic.

## Full fits: sampler × E₁

```{python}
#| label: fig-matrix
#| fig-cap: "Median (over the 11 spectra) worst-parameter bulk ESS per second of sampling, for every sampler × E₁ combination. Darker = faster."
M = V.groupby(["sampler", "E1"])["min_ess_bulk_per_s"].median().unstack()
M = M.reindex(index=[s for _, s in SAMPLERS], columns=[e for _, e in E1S])
fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(z=M.values, x=M.columns, y=M.index, colorscale=[[0, "#cde2fb"], [1, "#104281"]],
                           text=[[f"{v:.1f}" for v in row] for row in M.values], texttemplate="%{text}",
                           textfont=dict(size=16), colorbar=dict(title="ESS/s"), xgap=2, ygap=2,
                           hovertemplate="%{y} · %{x}: %{z:.1f} ESS/s<extra></extra>"))
fig.update_layout(height=320, yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed"), xaxis_title="E₁", yaxis_title="sampler")
show(fig)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-matrix
#| tbl-cap: "Per combination, medians over spectra. Gradient evaluations per iteration measure sampler efficiency (trajectory length). µs per gradient is the sampling wall time divided by all gradient evaluations, so it includes sampler overhead. Setup is compilation: numba (pm.sample, nutpie) or JAX JIT (NumPyro)."
g = V.groupby(["sampler", "E1"], sort=False)
T = pd.DataFrame({
    "sampling time (s)": g["time_sampling_s"].median(),
    "setup (s)": g["time_setup_s"].median(),
    "gradients / iteration": g["grads_per_iter"].median(),
    "µs / gradient (incl. sampler)": g["time_per_grad_us"].median(),
    "worst-param ESS": g["min_ess_bulk"].median(),
    "worst-param ESS/s": g["min_ess_bulk_per_s"].median(),
    "max R̂": g["max_rhat"].max(),
    "divergences": g["divergences"].sum(min_count=1),
}).reset_index()
T["_s"] = T["sampler"].map({s: i for i, (_, s) in enumerate(SAMPLERS)})
T["_e"] = T["E1"].map({e: i for i, (_, e) in enumerate(E1S)})
T = T.sort_values(["_s", "_e"]).drop(columns=["_s", "_e"])
show_table(fmt_table(T.rename(columns={"sampler": "Sampler", "E1": "E₁"}), 3))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-perspec
#| fig-cap: "Worst-parameter ESS/s per spectrum. Color = sampler, marker = E₁. Log scale; hover for the spectrum."
fig = go.Figure()
for b_, slab in SAMPLERS:
    for e_, elab in E1S:
        d = V[(V["backend"] == b_) & (V["errmodel"] == e_)]
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=d["min_ess_bulk_per_s"], y=[f"{slab} · {elab}"] * len(d), mode="markers",
            marker=dict(color=SCOLOR[b_], symbol=ESYM[e_], size=9, line=dict(color=SURFACE, width=1.5)),
            name=f"{slab} · {elab}", showlegend=False, customdata=d["sample_id"],
            hovertemplate="%{customdata}: %{x:.1f} ESS/s<extra>%{y}</extra>"))
fig.update_layout(height=430, xaxis=dict(type="log", title="worst-parameter ESS / s"),
                  yaxis=dict(categoryorder="array",
                             categoryarray=[f"{s} · {e}" for _, s in SAMPLERS for _, e in E1S][::-1]),
                  margin=dict(l=170))
show(fig)
```

```{python}
base = M.loc["pm.sample", "exact"]
best_s, best_e = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(M.values), M.shape)
best = M.values[best_s, best_e]
best_lab = f"{M.index[best_s]} + {M.columns[best_e]} E₁"
nut_fast = M.loc["nutpie", "fast"]
gpi = V.groupby("sampler")["grads_per_iter"].median()
upg = V.groupby(["sampler", "E1"])["time_per_grad_us"].median()
```

**What matters most.**

* The best combination is **`{python} best_lab`** at
  `{python} f"{best:.1f}"` ESS/s, `{python} f"{best/base:.1f}"`× the default
  (`pm.sample` + exact E₁, `{python} f"{base:.1f}"` ESS/s).
* **The sampler loop.** With the same compiled gradient, nutpie spends about
  `{python} f"{upg['nutpie','exact']:.0f}"` µs per gradient against
  `{python} f"{upg['pm.sample','exact']:.0f}"` µs for `pm.sample`, which runs
  NUTS in Python. Their trajectory lengths also differ, at a median
  `{python} f"{gpi['nutpie']:.1f}"` vs. `{python} f"{gpi['pm.sample']:.1f}"`
  gradients per iteration.
* **NumPyro on CPU** compiles the whole sampler with XLA, but its per-gradient
  cost depends entirely on how fast the JAX log-density is. With JAX's own
  `exp1` it is the slowest option by far. With the fast E₁ it is competitive.
* **E₁ choice.** The fast E₁ helps every sampler and costs no accuracy.
  Swamee–Ohija is never the fastest choice.

## Do all combinations sample the same posterior?

```{python}
#| label: tbl-agree-py
#| tbl-cap: "Largest standardized difference from Stan's posterior median ((median − Stan median) / Stan SD) over all spectra and parameters, and worst R̂, per combination."
ref = P[(P["backend"] == "stan") & (P["errmodel"] == "iid")].set_index(["sample_id", "param"])
rows = []
for b_, slab in SAMPLERS:
    for e_, elab in E1S:
        d = P[(P["backend"] == b_) & (P["errmodel"] == e_)].set_index(["sample_id", "param"])
        if d.empty:
            continue
        j = d.join(ref, rsuffix="_ref", how="inner")
        z = (j["q50"] - j["q50_ref"]) / j["sd_ref"]
        k = z.abs().idxmax()
        rows.append({"Sampler": slab, "E₁": elab, "max |z|": z.abs().max(), "where": f"{k[0]} · {k[1]}",
                     "median |z|": z.abs().median(), "max R̂": d["rhat"].max()})
show_table(fmt_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), 3))
```

All combinations target the same posterior. Differences from Stan are at the
Monte Carlo error level, except where the table shows otherwise.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A pitfall found along the way: `get_jaxified_logp(negative_logp=False)`

Despite its name, `pymc.sampling.jax.get_jaxified_logp(model, negative_logp=False)`
returns the **potential** $-\log p$. This is what PyMC passes to NumPyro as
`potential_fn`. Wrapping it as `potential_fn=lambda x: -logp(x)`, which the
name invites, makes NumPyro target $1/p$, an improper density. Nothing errors,
and the draws look like a plausible but wrong posterior. The first version of
`python/fit_pymc.py` had this bug. It was caught because σ disagreed with
the five reference backends.
:::

## Would a GPU (JAX) help?

*This section is reasoning, not measurement: no GPU was available.*

**For one spectrum: probably a small gain, or none.**

* **Each gradient is tiny.** It is a few hundred thousand floating-point
  operations on 2101 numbers, and NUTS needs each gradient before it can take
  the next step. A GPU would be limited by the fixed cost of launching work
  (about 5–10 µs per kernel), not by compute.
  * With NumPyro or BlackJAX, the whole NUTS loop is compiled and stays on the
    GPU, so there is no copying back and forth.
  * Each gradient might then take tens of µs, against
    `{python} f"{b['log-density + gradient','numba','fast']:.0f}"` µs on one CPU
    core here.
* **But PROSPECT needs float64.** The Stokes step subtracts nearly equal
  numbers ($v_b^{2(N-1)} - 1$), so float32 is risky for thick leaves. Consumer
  GPUs run float64 at 1/32 to 1/64 of their float32 speed. On an A100 or H100
  a single leaf might run a few times faster; on a gaming card, probably no
  faster.
* **The E₁ problem gets worse.** JAX's `exp1` evaluates every series
  iteration for every element, so the fast E₁ shown above becomes essential.
* **Compilation** adds several seconds per model (see the setup column above).

**For many spectra at once: this is where a GPU wins.**

* **Batching many leaves.** Running thousands of leaves (and chains) side by
  side with `jax.vmap`, e.g. all 340 ANGERS and LOPEX leaves, gives millions of
  band evaluations per step. That keeps a GPU busy, so the cost per leaf could
  drop by one to two orders of magnitude.
* **The better error models are GPU-shaped.** The GP discrepancy and the
  library-learned discrepancy recommended on [Error models](error-models.qmd)
  are mostly matrix products and low-rank updates. The hierarchical library
  model is one large model over many spectra.

**Recommendation.**

* **Single-leaf fits:** stay on the CPU with nutpie and the fast E₁, and
  consider fitting at a coarser wavelength step. Cost scales directly with
  the number of bands, and the residuals are correlated over tens of nm.
* **Library-scale or hierarchical models:** move to JAX on a GPU, with the
  fast E₁.
